question: About how long is a stretch usually held for?
answer: Around 20 to 30 seconds
distractors: Two seconds — a quick pull is all it takes
At least five minutes on each muscle
How long you hold it makes no difference
explanation: Twenty to thirty seconds is the usual guidance: long enough for the muscle to stop resisting and settle. Shorter holds aren't wasted, though — several short ones add up to much the same thing, so a quick stretch still counts.

question: What causes the ache that shows up a day or two after exercise?
answer: Unfamiliar work putting small amounts of stress through the fibers
distractors: Lactic acid left sitting in the muscle after the session
Losing too much water while you were moving
A joint that has been pushed further than it should have been
explanation: Work your muscles aren't used to — especially lowering things slowly — puts small amounts of stress through the fibers, and they rebuild a bit sturdier. It isn't lactic acid: that clears within about an hour of stopping, long before the ache arrives. Ordinary soreness eases over a few days; sharp pain that sticks around is worth having someone look at.

question: Which of these helps most people fall asleep faster?
answer: A slightly cooler room
distractors: A warm room, so your muscles stay relaxed
Bright light for the last hour before bed
A long nap in the late afternoon
explanation: Falling asleep depends on your body shedding a little heat, and a cool room makes that easy. A warm room sounds relaxing but works against the drop in core temperature that sleep actually waits for.

question: What's a simple way to check your balance at home?
answer: Standing on one foot for a few seconds
distractors: Timing how fast you can get up the stairs
Sitting down and lifting both feet off the floor
Seeing how far you can reach while sitting still
explanation: Standing on one foot makes your ankle, your eyes and your inner ear do work they normally share with the other leg, so any wobble shows up straight away. Next to a wall or a worktop is the sensible place to try it. Sitting tests take the one thing that matters — holding yourself up — out of the picture.

question: Why does a short walk after a meal help?
answer: Your working muscles take up some of the sugar from the food
distractors: The movement jostles food through your system faster
Walking pulls blood away from digestion, so it slows things down
The effect only appears once you've walked for about an hour
explanation: Muscles pull glucose out of the blood while they're working, so the rise after a meal is gentler. Ten minutes is enough to measure — you don't need an hour. And walking doesn't steal blood from digestion: that's the opposite of what happens.

question: What tends to happen to how flexible you feel across a day?
answer: Most people loosen up as the day goes on
distractors: You're at your stiffest in the middle of the afternoon
Flexibility is fixed — it doesn't shift hour to hour
You're loosest first thing, before you've moved much
explanation: Range of movement tends to improve through the day, tracking body temperature, which peaks in the late afternoon or early evening. It's a modest effect and it varies between people — worth knowing mainly so a stiff morning doesn't get read as a bad sign.

question: What makes a new habit most likely to stick?
answer: Tying it to something you already do every day
distractors: Starting as big as you can while motivation is high
Waiting until you can commit to doing it properly
Trusting yourself to remember it when a moment comes free
explanation: A habit needs a cue, and the most reliable cue is something already nailed down in your day — after you brush your teeth, before you put the kettle on. Starting big is the common instinct and usually the first thing to collapse: the size you can repeat beats the size that impresses you.

question: Roughly how big is an adult heart?
answer: About the size of a closed fist
distractors: About the size of a walnut in its shell
About the size of a football
About the size of a folded newspaper
explanation: It's a fist-sized pump sitting slightly left of center behind your breastbone, and it gets through something like 100,000 beats a day without being asked.

question: What usually happens after someone misses one day of a habit?
answer: Nothing much, as long as they pick it up again next time
distractors: The habit has to be rebuilt from the beginning
They need to do double the next day to stay even
The streak matters more than the habit underneath it
explanation: One missed day barely registers. What ends habits is treating the miss as proof the whole thing has failed — the getting-back-to-it is the part that matters, and it's available every single day.

question: What's unusual about climbing stairs, compared with walking on the flat?
answer: It asks your legs to lift your whole weight, step after step
distractors: It uses the same muscles but moves them through a smaller range
It works your calves and almost nothing else
It's gentler on the heart because you're going slower
explanation: Every step up is a small one-legged lift of your entire body weight, which is why a flight of stairs leaves you breathing harder than the same distance on the flat. It's also why stairs are one of the most useful things in an ordinary house.

question: Where do children pick up most of their movement habits?
answer: From watching the adults around them
distractors: From being told regularly that exercise matters
Mostly from PE lessons at school
From whichever sport their friends happen to play
explanation: Children copy what the adults around them actually do far more reliably than they follow what they're told — which is inconvenient, and also the most useful lever any parent has.

question: What improves balance fastest?
answer: Short goes at it, often
distractors: One long session every week or so
Staying off anything uneven until it improves
Practicing only with your eyes shut
explanation: Balance is a skill your nervous system rehearses, and rehearsal likes frequency more than duration. A minute while the kettle boils, most days, beats half an hour on a Sunday.

question: How does bone compare with steel?
answer: Bone resists squashing well for its weight; steel wins overall
distractors: Bone is stronger than steel by every measure anyone uses
Bone is weaker than steel by every measure anyone uses
They're close enough that bone has been used in engineering
explanation: "Pound for pound, stronger than steel" is a half-truth. Bone does well on compression for how light it is, which is the comparison that factoid is quietly making. Pull on it rather than squash it, or compare the two outright, and steel wins comfortably — bone's real trick is being strong enough while staying light enough to carry around.

question: What does a short daytime nap tend to do?
answer: Sharpen focus for a few hours without much cost to that night
distractors: Take the edge off tiredness but leave you groggy for the rest of the day
Work only for young children, whose sleep is different
Do nothing useful unless it runs a couple of hours
explanation: Ten to twenty minutes is the sweet spot: long enough to lift alertness, short enough that you don't surface out of deep sleep feeling worse than you went in. The groggy-nap problem is a length problem, not a nap problem.

question: Which of these is the ordinary kind of post-exercise soreness?
answer: A general achy tiredness that eases over a few days
distractors: A sharp pain that arrives suddenly during a movement
Swelling around a joint that keeps getting bigger
Not being able to put weight on something at all
explanation: Dull, spread-out, and fading by itself is the normal kind. Sharp, sudden, swelling, or something you can't use — those are your body asking for a different response, which is to stop and have someone take a look.

question: Which part of a slow breath is the part that calms you down?
answer: Breathing out for longer than you breathe in
distractors: Filling your lungs as full as they will go
Holding the breath at the top for as long as you can
Breathing quickly so more oxygen reaches your brain
explanation: Your heart speeds up slightly as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out, so a long, unhurried exhale is the bit that actually settles things. Breath-holding contests do the opposite, and are genuinely risky in water — never a calming technique. You also aren't short of oxygen when you're stressed, so breathing faster doesn't help.

question: What happens when someone puts a name to what they're feeling?
answer: It usually gets a little easier to handle
distractors: It makes the feeling stronger, by focusing on it
It works only for feelings you have had before
It replaces the feeling with a different one
explanation: Putting a feeling into words — "I'm frustrated", "I'm nervous" — reliably takes some of the heat out of it. It doesn't make the feeling worse by naming it, which is the usual worry. It also doesn't make it vanish; it just turns something vague into something you can think about.

question: Why does a walk help when your head is full of the same thought going round?
answer: Moving and new scenery interrupt the loop it's running in
distractors: Walking burns off the energy the worry was feeding on
It tires you enough that the thought stops mattering much
Extra blood reaches your brain, which helps solve the problem
explanation: Going round and round on the same thought is a loop, and loops are broken by interruption more than by effort. New things to look at and a body with something to do give your attention somewhere else to be. It isn't about using up energy or wearing yourself out — a gentle ten minutes works as well as a hard hour.

question: What does writing down what's on your mind tend to do?
answer: It forces the tangle into an order, which gives it a shape
distractors: It solves the problem you were writing about
It works only if you are sure nobody will read it
It works only for people who find writing easy
explanation: A worry can sit in your head as one big shapeless thing. Writing forces it into one word after another, which is why people often find the tangle is smaller than it felt. The writing doesn't have to be good, and it doesn't solve anything by itself — it just makes the thing a shape you can look at.

question: What is a "growth mindset"?
answer: Treating ability as something practice changes
distractors: Believing anyone can be excellent at anything, given enough want
Staying positive about a result however it actually went
Measuring your progress against people slightly ahead of you
explanation: It's the belief that getting better is a thing you do, not a thing you are. Worth being precise about, because it gets stretched into "you can be anything", which isn't the claim and isn't true. It's narrower and more useful than that: being bad at something today is information about today.

question: What are the nerves and the racing heart before something new actually for?
answer: Getting your body ready to do something that matters
distractors: Warning you that the thing is likely to go badly
A sign you haven't prepared enough for it
Something that goes away once you're properly good at things
explanation: The pounding heart and the fizzy stomach are your body getting ready, and they look almost identical whether the thing ahead is frightening or exciting. People who are very good at something still get them — they've mostly just stopped reading them as a warning.

question: What happens to concentration when you work at one thing for a long stretch?
answer: It drops off gradually, and a short break restores some of it
distractors: It holds steady as long as you're interested in the task
It improves the longer you stay with one thing
It only drops once you start to feel physically tired
explanation: Attention on a single task decays — measurably, within tens of minutes — and it does it whether or not you notice or feel tired. A few minutes away restores part of it. Breaks aren't time taken out of the work; they're part of how the work keeps being any good.

question: What makes a child most likely to keep moving as they get older?
answer: Having found something they actually enjoy doing
distractors: Being good at a sport early on
Being reminded often that exercise is important
Having started younger than everyone else
explanation: Enjoyment predicts whether someone is still moving years later better than talent, early starts or encouragement do. Being good at something young is a weaker signal than people expect — plenty of early stars stop, and plenty of people who were never picked first are still walking, swimming and dancing at sixty.

question: What does cheering for someone do that comparing them to someone else doesn't?
answer: It keeps attention on what they did, not where they rank
distractors: It motivates them to try harder and win the next one
It works well with children but stops landing with adults
It stops them noticing when a day has genuinely gone badly
explanation: Comparison quietly changes the subject from "did I move today" to "am I winning", and only one of those is a thing you can keep doing for life. Cheering keeps the subject where it started. It works on everyone, and it doesn't require pretending a bad day was a good one.

question: Roughly how much of what children learn about being active comes from watching, rather than being told?
answer: Most of it
distractors: About half of it
Very little — instruction matters more
None — it's mainly decided by personality
explanation: Children read behavior far more accurately than they absorb instruction, which is why the walk you take on a day you don't feel like it does more than any amount of explaining. Personality plays a part, but it isn't the main lever, and the main lever is one adults are holding already.

question: Why can a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old do the same walk together?
answer: Because walking has no single right speed, so both can be working
distractors: Because walking is gentle enough that it barely counts for either
Because children have much less stamina than adults
Because fitness stops mattering once you are past about fifty
explanation: Effort is relative. The same walk can be gentle for one person and a genuine workout for another, and both get something from it. Children actually have plenty of stamina — what they have less of is the pacing to spend it evenly.

question: Why do children sometimes get clumsier during a growth spurt?
answer: Their limbs got longer faster than the brain's map updated
distractors: Growing uses energy that would otherwise go to coordination
Bones grow before muscles do, which makes movement stiffer
Growing children lose balance practice while they're resting
explanation: Your brain holds a map of how long your arms and legs are, built from practice. When the limbs get longer quickly, the map is briefly out of date and things get knocked over. It sorts itself out with ordinary use — the map updates by moving.

question: Does lifting weights stunt a child's growth?
answer: No — it's an old myth, and sensible strength work is fine
distractors: Yes — it compresses the growth plates and costs final height
Yes, but only for children who start before about twelve
Nobody knows — it would be unethical to run the study
explanation: This one has been studied a lot, and the height claim doesn't hold up. It probably came from confusing cause and effect — smaller children were once more likely to be put in weightlifting. What genuinely matters is how something is done: sensible loads and someone showing you how, the same as any other skill.

question: Why can children often play for hours without seeming to need a rest?
answer: They recover between bursts much faster than adults do
distractors: They have more stamina than adults overall
They don't notice tiredness until much later
Their muscles are more efficient than an adult's
explanation: Children play in bursts rather than at a steady pace, and they bounce back between bursts remarkably quickly. Their overall endurance isn't higher than a fit adult's — the recovery is what's different, which is why the adult is the one asking to sit down.

question: What happens to balance as people get older, if nothing is done about it?
answer: It fades slowly, and practicing it slows the fade a great deal
distractors: It stays the same until quite late in life, then drops suddenly
It's fixed by your genes and can't be practiced
It improves, because of all the years of practice
explanation: Balance behaves like any other skill: use keeps it, disuse loses it. The drift is gradual and it responds well to being practiced, which is why standing on one leg while the kettle boils is a genuinely useful minute at any age.

question: Why does the same hill get easier after a few weeks of walking it?
answer: Your heart pushes more blood per beat, so it costs less
distractors: Your lungs grow bigger and hold more air than they did
Your legs learn the route, so the same hill feels shorter
Your body adapts to need less oxygen than it used to
explanation: The main change is in the pump: a fitter heart moves more blood with each beat, so it doesn't have to beat as fast to do the same job. Lungs don't change size much with training, and you don't need less oxygen — you just deliver it better.

question: What does a resting heart rate settling lower over months usually mean?
answer: The heart is doing the same work with fewer beats
distractors: The heart is getting weaker and beating less forcefully
There's less blood in circulation than there was
It's random, and doesn't track fitness at all
explanation: Fewer beats for the same output is what getting fitter looks like from the outside. It's one of the few changes you can actually watch happen — count for a minute now, and again in two months of regular walking.

question: What's the simplest way to tell whether you're working at an easy pace?
answer: You can hold a conversation, but not comfortably sing
distractors: You've not started sweating yet, whatever the pace feels like
Your heart rate is somewhere under about 120 beats
You could keep the same pace up for at least an hour
explanation: The talk test costs nothing and needs no watch: speaking in sentences means steady, singing means easy, and struggling for words means hard. Sweating depends mostly on the weather, and a single heart-rate number fits almost nobody.

question: Which kind of ache is worth stopping for?
answer: A sharp pain in one specific spot, especially in a joint
distractors: A general heaviness in the muscles you've been using
Being out of breath more than you expected
Feeling wobbly-legged for a few minutes afterwards
explanation: Spread-out, dull and fading is the ordinary kind. Sharp, pinpointed, and coming from a joint is the kind that wants attention now rather than tomorrow. Being out of breath or briefly wobbly is just effort, and it passes.

question: Something still hurts the next morning. What's the sensible move?
answer: Do something gentler today and see how it is tomorrow
distractors: Push through it, because stopping loses your progress
Rest completely until there's no feeling at all
Repeat exactly what caused it, so the body adapts
explanation: Gentler, not nothing, and check again tomorrow. Complete rest is rarely needed and often slows things down, and doing exactly the thing that hurt is how a small niggle becomes a long one. If it's still there in a few days, or getting worse, that's the point to ask someone who can look at it.

question: What's the most useful thing to do before moving about in hot weather?
answer: Drink before you're thirsty and plan somewhere shaded to stop
distractors: Wear more layers so you sweat the heat out faster
Skip drinking during, so you aren't sloshing about
Go harder than usual, since the heat has warmed you up already
explanation: Thirst lags behind what you've actually lost, so drinking early is the useful habit. Extra layers trap the heat your body is trying to shed, which is the opposite of helping. And heat makes everything cost more, so it's a day to do less, not more.

question: Why is jumping into cold water risky even for a strong swimmer?
answer: Cold water makes you gasp, which is the danger below the surface
distractors: Cold muscles cramp the moment they hit the water
Cold water is denser, so it's much harder to stay afloat
The danger builds with how long you stay in, not on entry
explanation: The first thing cold water does is make you gasp and breathe fast, whether you want to or not, and a gasp underwater is the actual danger — not the temperature or how long you stay. Getting in slowly gives that reflex a minute to settle.

question: A movement doesn't work for your body today. What's the best response?
answer: Do a smaller version, or something that asks the same of you
distractors: Skip the session, since a partial one doesn't really count
Do it anyway, and accept that it won't be comfortable
Wait until whatever is limiting you has cleared up properly
explanation: Almost every movement has a smaller cousin: a squat to a chair, a push-up against a wall, a march instead of a jump. The smaller version is not a lesser session — it's the same session, sized for the day you're actually having.

question: What does a wall push-up have in common with a floor push-up?
answer: The same muscles in the same pattern, with less of your weight on them
distractors: Nothing — it's a different movement that happens to look similar
It's harder, because your feet have less grip
It only helps as practice for the real one
explanation: Standing further from the wall puts more of you into it, so it's one movement with a dial on it rather than a beginner's substitute. That's true of most things: the angle, the range, or how much of you is involved is usually the adjustable part.

question: What helps most if you have to sit for most of the day?
answer: Getting up briefly and often, rather than one long session later
distractors: One hard workout at the end of the day
Sitting up straighter for the whole time
Nothing much — sitting is unavoidable, so it can't be helped
explanation: Breaking up the sitting matters somewhat separately from how much you exercise: standing up every half hour or so does something a single evening session doesn't replace. Posture helps comfort, but it's the getting up that shows in the measurements.

question: Why do your eyes feel tired after a long stretch of screen time?
answer: Close focus holds one muscle still, and you blink less often
distractors: Screens emit a kind of light your eyes can't process well
Your eyes work harder at a screen than they do outdoors
The brightness slowly wears away the surface of the eye
explanation: Close focus is a held position, like any other held position, and people blink roughly half as often while reading a screen — which is why eyes feel dry as well as tired. Looking at something far away for a few seconds lets the muscle let go. The screen isn't damaging anything.

question: Why is catching a ball harder than it looks?
answer: Your brain predicts where it will be, rather than reacting
distractors: The ball moves faster than your eyes are able to track it
Your hands respond more slowly than the rest of your body
It depends mostly on how strong and quick your grip is
explanation: Nerve signals take time, so reacting to where the ball is would always be too late. Your brain is running a prediction and putting your hand where the ball is going to be. Practice mostly improves the prediction, which is why catching gets easier without your hands getting any faster.

question: What happens when you learn a physical skill well enough to stop thinking about it?
answer: Control shifts to parts of the brain you needn't attend to
distractors: The movement gets stored in the muscles that perform it
Your brain hands it to the spinal cord and stops tracking it
You've reached the point where it can no longer improve
explanation: "Muscle memory" is a good name for a real thing in the wrong place — muscles store nothing. What happens is that control moves to circuits that run without your attention, which is why you can hold a conversation while cycling, and why thinking too hard about it makes you wobble.

question: Which is the largest muscle in your body?
answer: The one you sit on
distractors: The one at the front of your thigh
The one in your upper back
The one in your calf
explanation: The gluteus maximus is the biggest muscle you own, and it does the heavy work in standing up, climbing stairs and pushing off the ground. The thigh and back muscles are strong, but they're not the largest.

question: What connects a muscle to a bone?
answer: A tendon
distractors: A ligament
Cartilage
A nerve
explanation: Tendons anchor muscle to bone. You can feel one on the back of your ankle — the thick cord above your heel is the biggest tendon in your body.

question: What connects one bone to another at a joint?
answer: A ligament
distractors: A tendon
A muscle
A blood vessel
explanation: Ligaments tie bone to bone and keep joints from wandering out of place. Tendons do the other job — muscle to bone.

question: How many bones does a typical adult have?
explanation: Babies start with around 300 separate bones, and many fuse while growing — which is how you arrive at roughly 206 as an adult. The number isn't exactly the same for everyone; a few people have an extra rib or a spare bone in a foot.

question: Roughly what share of your bones are in your hands and feet?
answer: More than half
distractors: About a quarter
About a tenth
Around a twentieth
explanation: 27 bones in each hand and 26 in each foot — 106 of about 206. If you half-remember "a quarter of your bones are in your feet", that's the feet alone; add the hands and you're past half. Gripping and stepping need many small bones, not big ones.

question: What's happening inside a bone right now?
answer: Cells are removing old bone and laying down new bone, constantly
distractors: Nothing — bone is finished material, like a shell
It's still growing, but only until you stop getting taller
It slowly hardens throughout life and doesn't change otherwise
explanation: Bone is rebuilt continuously, at every age. That's how a break knits, how bone thickens where it's loaded, and why it thins when nothing pulls on it. Growing taller stops; rebuilding doesn't.

question: What's inside your larger bones?
answer: Marrow, which makes blood cells
distractors: Solid mineral all the way through
Mostly air, to keep them light
A fluid that cushions impacts
explanation: Bone marrow is a factory. The red blood cells carrying oxygen around you right now were made inside your bones. Bones are light because of their honeycomb structure, not because they're hollow.

question: What lets your joints move smoothly instead of grinding?
answer: Cartilage caps and a slippery fluid between
distractors: A layer of muscle cushioning the bone ends
Tiny pockets of air acting as a buffer
Bones shaped so that they never quite touch
explanation: Cartilage caps the bone ends and joint fluid sits between them. The combination is slicker than ice on ice — and the fluid spreads better the more you move, which is why joints feel easier a few minutes into a walk.

question: What kind of joint is your elbow?
answer: A hinge, opening one way like a door
distractors: A ball-and-socket, like your shoulder
A joint that slides rather than pivots
A fixed joint, held together by the forearm bones
explanation: The elbow is a hinge, so it bends one way. Turning your palm over isn't the elbow rotating — it's the two forearm bones crossing over each other.

question: Which of these is a ball-and-socket joint?
answer: The shoulder
distractors: The knee
The ankle
The jaw
explanation: Shoulders and hips are ball-and-socket, which is why your arm can draw a full circle. The knee is a hinge with a little rotation, and the jaw is a hinge that also slides forward.

question: How do muscles create movement?
answer: They pull, by getting shorter
distractors: They push bones apart from the inside
They stiffen and act as levers
They shorten and lengthen in equal measure
explanation: A muscle can only pull. That's the whole reason they come in pairs: your bicep pulls your forearm up, and your tricep has to pull it back down again.

question: Where is the smallest bone in your body?
answer: In your ear
distractors: In your little toe
In your nose
In your wrist
explanation: The stapes, deep in the middle ear, is around 3mm — smaller than a grain of rice. It passes sound vibrations inward, and it's the last link in a chain of three tiny bones.

question: Which is the longest bone in your body?
answer: The thigh bone
distractors: The upper arm bone
The shin bone
The collarbone
explanation: The femur runs from hip to knee and is roughly a quarter of your total height — measure a friend's and you can estimate how tall they are.

question: Where does blood go straight after leaving the right side of your heart?
answer: To your lungs
distractors: To your brain
Out to your legs and arms
To your stomach
explanation: Blood takes a short loop to the lungs for oxygen, returns to the heart, and only then goes out to the rest of you. It's two pumps sharing one organ, which is why the left side has the thicker wall.

question: What does your blood pick up in your lungs?
answer: Oxygen, in exchange for carbon dioxide
distractors: Sugar, from the food you've eaten
Water, to keep the blood thin
Salt, which regulates blood pressure
explanation: It's a swap, and it happens across walls thinner than tissue paper: carbon dioxide out, oxygen in. Sugar and salt join the blood much further along, from your gut.

question: What is your pulse, exactly?
answer: Blood pushing an artery wall as the wave arrives
distractors: The heart muscle itself, felt through the skin
A nerve firing in time with every heartbeat
Blood changing direction as it rounds a corner
explanation: Every beat sends a pressure wave down your arteries, and what you feel at your wrist is that wave arriving — a fraction of a second after the beat itself. It travels far faster than the blood does.

question: Which muscle does most of the work when you breathe in?
answer: The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under the lungs
distractors: The lungs themselves, which squeeze inward
The heart, which shares the same cavity
The stomach muscles, working downward
explanation: Lungs contain no muscle at all. The diaphragm pulls down, the space inside your chest gets bigger, and air rushes in to fill it — you don't suck air in so much as make room for it.

question: How long does a red blood cell take to travel all the way around your body?
answer: About a minute
distractors: About an hour
About a day
About a week
explanation: At rest, one full lap takes roughly a minute. During hard exercise it's considerably quicker — the same blood, going round several times faster.

question: What often happens to resting heart rate after months of regular activity?
answer: It tends to settle a little lower
distractors: It tends to creep upward as the heart works more
It stops varying and holds one steady number
It rises during training months and falls after stopping
explanation: A well-practiced heart moves more blood per squeeze, so it needs fewer beats while you're sitting still. It's one of the few fitness changes you can watch happen — count for a minute now, and again in two months.

question: Why do you breathe faster during exercise?
answer: Your muscles use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
distractors: Your lungs hold less air once you've started moving
Faster breathing is mainly how your body sheds its heat
Your heart briefly pauses between the harder beats
explanation: More work means more oxygen used and more carbon dioxide made, and your breathing rises to match. Exactly how your body knows to do it so quickly is still argued over by physiologists — the sensing is more complicated than the arithmetic.

question: Which is true about your two lungs?
answer: The left is slightly smaller, making room for the heart
distractors: The right is noticeably smaller than the left
They're identical, like your two kidneys
They take turns, one resting while the other works
explanation: Your heart sits slightly left of center, so the left lung has a scooped-out notch and two lobes while the right has three. Both work all the time.

question: What color is the blood inside your veins?
answer: Red — darker when it's carrying less oxygen
distractors: Blue until it meets air, and then it turns red
Bluish while it flows, red only once it clots
Clear, taking its color from whatever it carries
explanation: Blood is red everywhere: dark red when it has given its oxygen away, bright red fresh from the lungs. It never turns blue. Veins look blue because of how skin scatters light, not because of what's inside them.

question: Laid end to end, how far would one person's blood vessels stretch?
answer: Tens of thousands of miles
distractors: A few hundred yards
About a mile
A few hundred miles
explanation: Estimates run to tens of thousands of miles. Almost all of that length is capillaries far finer than a hair — the big vessels are a rounding error in the total.

question: What are the tiniest blood vessels called?
answer: Capillaries
distractors: Arteries
Veins
Valves
explanation: Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells pass through almost single file. That's the point — it's where oxygen is actually handed over, and it needs the cells close to the wall.

question: What stops blood flowing backwards in your veins?
answer: One-way valves along their length
distractors: The constant forward push from the heart
Their narrowness, which stops flow reversing
Surrounding bone, which holds them in shape
explanation: Veins have tiny one-way flaps. By the time blood reaches them the heart's push is nearly spent, so the flaps matter — and every squeeze of your calf muscles while walking pushes blood up past the next one.

question: What does the word 'cardio' actually refer to?
answer: The heart
distractors: The lungs
The legs
The joints
explanation: It's from kardia, the Greek for heart. "Cardio" is simply anything that keeps your heart working steadily for a stretch — which is why a brisk walk counts and a sprint-and-stop game counts differently.

question: What does good posture mostly depend on?
answer: Changing position often
distractors: Holding one correct position all day
Keeping your back straight at all times
Sitting rather than standing, which loads the spine less
explanation: There's a saying among physiotherapists: the best posture is your next one. Bodies cope with variety far better than with any single position held for hours — including the one that looks correct.

question: What are your arms doing when you walk normally?
answer: Swinging opposite the legs, cancelling your hips' twist
distractors: Swinging with the same-side leg, adding to the stride
Very little — it's habit more than anything useful
Helping you breathe by opening out the ribcage
explanation: Right arm forward with left leg is no accident: the counter-swing cancels the twist your hips put into your spine, and it makes walking measurably cheaper. Hold your arms still for a minute and you'll feel the difference.

question: What's the main job of your core muscles?
answer: Holding your spine steady while you move
distractors: Bending you forward, in the way a sit-up does
Pulling your shoulders back into a better position
Helping you breathe out with real force
explanation: Your core mostly works by resisting movement rather than creating it. It's the steady base everything else pushes against — which is why carrying shopping in one hand is a core exercise and sit-ups are only part of the picture.

question: Why do people naturally take shorter steps on ice?
answer: A short step needs less grip from the ground to stop you sliding
distractors: Short steps keep your feet in contact with the ground for longer
Cold stiffens the legs, which shortens the stride automatically
Short steps are faster, which gets you off the ice sooner
explanation: A long stride pushes you forward and backward as much as up, and it's that sideways push that needs grip. Shorten the step and you need less of it. Nobody teaches you this — your balance system works it out within a step or two.

question: Standing up from a chair is basically which movement?
answer: A squat
distractors: A press
A pull
A twist
explanation: Sitting down and standing up is a squat you already do dozens of times a day. Practicing squats is mostly practicing getting out of chairs — which is exactly why it stays useful for the next sixty years.

question: What does 'coordination' actually mean?
answer: Getting different body parts to act in the right order
distractors: Being able to move faster than the people around you
Having enough strength to control a movement properly
Being flexible enough to get into almost any position
explanation: Coordination is timing more than power. Catching a ball takes almost no strength — it takes your eyes, arm and hand agreeing on a moment.

question: What makes a heavy object feel lighter to carry?
answer: Holding it close to your body
distractors: Holding it out in front of you
Holding it above your head
Holding it out to one side
explanation: The further a load sits from you, the longer the lever it has against your back. Same box, same weight, far more work — which is the real reason "lift with your legs" is usually advice about where the box is, not how you bend.

question: What happens to most people's feet over the course of a day?
answer: They swell slightly
distractors: They shrink slightly
They stay the same but get colder
They flatten as the arch tires
explanation: Feet swell through the day, which is why shoes that fit at nine in the morning can feel snug by the evening. It's a good argument for trying shoes on late in the day.

question: Why does walking downhill feel easy but leave your legs sore?
answer: The muscles are working while being stretched, which causes more soreness
distractors: Going downhill uses almost no muscle, so they're caught out
It's harder on the heart, and the legs pay for that
Downhill and uphill are the same — the soreness comes from the distance
explanation: Going down, your leg muscles act as brakes: working hard while being lengthened. Your lungs get an easy ride and your thighs settle the bill tomorrow. It's the single biggest cause of next-day soreness in ordinary walking.

question: What is proprioception?
answer: Knowing where your body parts are without looking
distractors: Your sense of balance while in water
How quickly you can react to something you see
The sense that tells you which way up you are
explanation: Close your eyes and touch your nose. Nothing told you where your finger was or where your nose was — that's a whole sense most people never notice they have, and it's why you can walk without watching your feet.

question: What does your body use to work out which way is up?
answer: Your inner ear, your eyes, and pressure sensors in your feet
distractors: Your inner ear alone, which is the organ built for it
Your eyes alone, measuring against the horizon
Your sense of where your limbs are, working on its own
explanation: Three sources vote, and your brain goes with the majority. Seasickness is what happens when they disagree — your inner ear says moving, your eyes say the cabin is still.

question: Why does walking feel effortless to most adults?
answer: Your brain automated it years ago, with practice
distractors: Walking genuinely takes very little muscle work
Gravity does most of the work once you're moving
Your legs run on reflexes that don't involve the brain
explanation: Walking is a hard balancing problem — robots are still not very good at it. Yours was solved so long ago that you can do it while reading your phone, which is the only reason it feels like nothing.

question: How do muscles actually get stronger?
answer: They repair after being worked, and come back slightly sturdier
distractors: They stretch permanently, so they can pull over a longer distance
They gain extra fibers each time they're worked hard
They store more fuel, which makes each pull stronger
explanation: The work is the signal, not the result. The building happens afterwards, while you're going about your day and sleeping. You don't grow new fibers in any number that matters — the ones you have get better at their job.

question: What does 'progressive overload' mean?
answer: Gradually asking for a bit more than last time
distractors: Going as hard as you possibly can each session
Repeating exactly the same thing until it feels easy
Adding a new exercise every week to keep things fresh
explanation: One more repetition, a slightly longer hold, a little more range. Bodies adapt to what they're asked for, so the ask has to creep up — but creeping is the operative word. Going flat out every time isn't progression, it's just a hard day repeated.

question: What's the difference between flexibility and mobility?
answer: How far a joint can be moved, versus moving it there yourself
distractors: Two words for the same measurement, used interchangeably
Flexibility describes muscles, mobility describes joints
Mobility is just flexibility measured once you're warm
explanation: You can be flexible without being mobile: able to be put into a position, but not able to get there under your own power and hold it. The second one is what's actually useful when you reach for something on a high shelf.

question: Which kind of stretching fits a warm-up best?
answer: Moving stretches, like leg swings and arm circles
distractors: Long held stretches, to lengthen the muscle first
Stretches held right to the edge of discomfort
No stretching — warm up with the activity itself
explanation: Moving stretches wake up the muscles you're about to use and rehearse the range you'll need. Long holds sit better at the end. Warming up with the activity itself isn't wrong, incidentally — it's just slower to get you there.

question: Can you build real strength without any equipment?
answer: Yes — your weight is resistance, and muscles can't tell
distractors: Only up to a point, after which weights become necessary
Only for the upper body, since the legs already carry you
Not really — bodyweight work builds endurance, not strength
explanation: Muscles respond to tension and have no idea where it came from. A push-up and a bench press are the same conversation in different words. What bodyweight work makes harder is adding load gradually — which is a logistics problem, not a physiology one.

question: What does grip strength tend to reflect?
answer: Overall body strength, reasonably well
distractors: The size of your forearms, and not much else
How much you use your hands day to day
Hand size, which sets how much you can squeeze
explanation: Grip tracks whole-body strength closely enough that researchers use a hand squeeze as a quick stand-in for it. Forearm muscle is certainly part of the story — it's just not the whole of it.

question: What happens in a muscle when you hold a stretch for a while?
answer: Your nervous system eases off, and allows more range
distractors: The muscle fibers themselves get permanently longer
Small tears form, and heal at the new length
Blood fills the muscle, which softens it temporarily
explanation: Most of what limits a stretch is your nervous system guarding the position, not the muscle running out of length. Your body decides the position is safe and stops resisting — which is exactly why forcing a stretch works so badly.

question: Which is true about working against resistance and your bones?
answer: It keeps bone strong — bone responds to load
distractors: It builds muscle but leaves the bone unchanged
Only running and jumping have any effect on bone
Bone density is set by diet rather than by movement
explanation: Bone lays down more material where the stress is. Astronauts lose bone density in orbit for precisely this reason — nothing pulls on them. Diet matters too, but it's the pulling that tells the bone where to put it.

question: What's an isometric exercise?
answer: Holding a position without moving, like a plank
distractors: Lifting something as explosively as you can
Moving through a full range under control
Any exercise done without equipment
explanation: The muscle is working flat out while nothing visibly happens. A wall sit looks like doing nothing and feels like anything but — which makes it a useful option when space or noise is a problem.

question: Why do people feel stronger after a few sessions, before muscles have changed?
answer: Your nervous system is learning to switch more fibers on at once
distractors: Muscle grows faster in the first weeks than later on
The bones adapt first, giving the muscles a better anchor
It's mostly confidence — the strength itself hasn't changed
explanation: Early gains are your brain learning to recruit more fibers and time them better. Real, measurable, and much faster than muscle growth — which is why the first few weeks of anything feel so encouraging.

question: Which is true about flexibility?
answer: It's mostly specific to each joint
distractors: Being flexible in one place means you're flexible everywhere
It's fixed at birth and can't meaningfully change
It depends mainly on how long your limbs are
explanation: Flexibility is local. Someone who can fold in half at the hips may have stiff shoulders, and neither tells you anything about the other. It's also trainable at any age, just slowly.

question: Which muscles tend to get tight in people who sit for long stretches?
answer: The ones at the front of the hips
distractors: The ones along the back of the neck
The ones in the forearms
The ones around the ribs
explanation: Sitting holds your hip flexors short for hours, and muscles adapt to the length they spend most of their time at. Standing up and opening the hips is the counter-move, and it takes about ten seconds.

question: When does most muscle repair happen?
answer: Between sessions, not during them
distractors: During the session, as the muscle is worked
Only on the days you train
Continuously, at the same rate whatever you do
explanation: Training is the request; recovery is where it gets built. Rest days aren't time off from the process — they're the half of it where something actually changes.

question: What is your body busy doing while you sleep?
answer: Repairing tissue, filing memories and releasing hormones
distractors: Shutting down almost entirely to save energy
Digesting, and very little else
Resting the brain while the body carries on as usual
explanation: Sleep is the body's maintenance window, and it's busy. Tissue repair, hormone release and memory filing all cluster into those hours — the brain in particular is nowhere near switched off.

question: What does sleep do after you practice a new skill?
answer: It helps lock in what you practiced
distractors: It has no effect — only waking practice counts
It clears the practice out, to make room for the next day
It helps only if you sleep straight after practicing
explanation: Your brain replays the day's practice while you sleep, and the replay is part of the learning. It's why a move you kept fumbling can feel oddly easier the next morning without you having touched it again.

question: What does morning light do for your body?
answer: It sets your internal body clock for the day
distractors: It mainly helps by warming you up
It only matters for people who struggle to sleep
It affects your eyes but not the rest of you
explanation: Some cells in your eyes aren't for seeing at all — they just report how bright it is, and that report is what sets your clock. Morning light is the strongest signal you'll get all day.

question: What does bright light in the evening tend to do?
answer: It makes sleep harder to fall into
distractors: It helps, by tiring the eyes out
It affects only what you dream about
It matters far less than what time you go to bed
explanation: Your body reads bright light as daytime, whatever the clock says. For most of human history evening light meant fire — dim and orange — so a bright room at ten at night is a fairly new message to send.

question: What happens to your heart rate while you're asleep?
answer: It drops below your daytime resting rate
distractors: It rises, because the body is busy repairing
It holds at exactly your daytime resting rate
It swings widely, with no pattern to it
explanation: Your lowest heart rate of the entire day almost always happens while you're asleep, without you doing a single thing. It does rise during dreaming sleep, which is part of why the night isn't flat.

question: Which stage of sleep is famous for vivid dreams?
answer: REM sleep, named for the eye movements
distractors: Deep slow-wave sleep, early in the night
The first few minutes, as you drift off
Light dozing, just before you wake
explanation: REM stands for rapid eye movement, and your eyes really do flick about behind closed lids. Meanwhile most of your body is temporarily held still — which is probably just as well.

question: Roughly how often does a sleep cycle repeat through the night?
answer: About every 90 minutes
distractors: About every 20 minutes
About every 4 hours
Once, over the whole night
explanation: You cycle through lighter and deeper sleep roughly every 90 minutes, and the mix shifts as the night goes on: more deep sleep early, more dreaming later. Losing the last two hours isn't the same as losing the first two.

question: How does a child's sleep need compare with an adult's?
answer: Children need noticeably more
distractors: Children and adults need about the same
Children need less, because they nap in the day
It depends entirely on the individual, not on age
explanation: Growing bodies and fast-learning brains run on more sleep. Teenagers also have a body clock that genuinely shifts later, so a teenager sleeping in is biology rather than character.

question: What does keeping roughly the same sleep and wake time help with?
answer: It lets your body clock settle into a rhythm it can predict
distractors: It mainly helps you fall asleep faster on the first night
It matters for athletes but makes little difference otherwise
It makes mornings harder, by removing the chance to catch up
explanation: Your body starts preparing for sleep and for waking before either happens — but only if it can predict when. Regularity is the thing that makes it predictable, which is why it often beats an extra half hour.

question: What is 'active recovery'?
answer: Easy movement, like a gentle walk, on a lighter day
distractors: Stretching thoroughly until the soreness clears
Complete rest, with as little movement as possible
A short, hard session to flush the muscles through
explanation: Easy movement keeps blood circulating without adding to the workload. Most people find a gentle walk leaves them feeling better than sitting still — and better than trying to stretch it out, which does less than its reputation suggests.

question: What happens in the brain during deep sleep?
answer: Slow, coordinated waves sweep across it, and memories get filed
distractors: It shuts down almost completely to conserve energy
It runs faster than while awake, working through the day
Activity becomes random, which is what produces dreams
explanation: Deep sleep has a signature: large slow waves moving across the whole brain, during which the day's experiences get consolidated. Whether sleep also flushes waste out of brain tissue is genuinely argued over at the moment — a well-known 2013 finding was directly contradicted in 2024, and it isn't settled.

question: Why do people often feel groggy after a long nap?
answer: They surfaced out of a deeper stage than a short nap reaches
distractors: Long naps dry you out, and that's what causes the fogginess
The body takes a while to warm back up after lying still
It happens at random, and isn't related to how long you nap
explanation: That heavy, foggy feeling has a name: sleep inertia. It comes from surfacing out of deep sleep rather than light sleep, which is why ten or twenty minutes leaves you sharp and an hour can leave you worse than before. It passes.

question: What does sleep do for the following day's mood?
answer: It changes how strongly you react to things the next day
distractors: It affects tired muscles, but not mood
It matters only after several bad nights in a row
Mood and sleep move independently of each other
explanation: After poor sleep the emotional part of the brain reacts more strongly and the calming part has less grip on it. Small things genuinely do feel bigger — it isn't a failure of perspective, and one bad night is enough to show it.

question: Roughly how much of your body is water?
answer: About half to two-thirds
distractors: About a fifth
About a tenth
Around nine-tenths
explanation: Somewhere around half to two-thirds, depending on the person. Even your bones are roughly a fifth water — the dry-looking parts aren't especially dry.

question: What is sweat mainly for?
answer: Cooling you, as it evaporates off your skin
distractors: Cooling you, by carrying heat out in the liquid itself
Cleaning the skin of what the day has put on it
Getting rid of things the body doesn't want
explanation: Sweat only cools you when it evaporates — the change from liquid to vapour is what carries the heat away. Sweat that drips off does almost nothing, which is exactly why a breeze feels wonderful and a humid day feels unbearable.

question: Which food group is your body's quickest source of energy?
answer: Carbohydrates
distractors: Protein
Fats
Vitamins
explanation: Carbohydrates break down into sugars your cells can use almost immediately. Fat carries more energy but takes longer to get at, and protein is building material that your body would rather not burn.

question: What is protein mainly used for?
answer: Building and repairing tissue
distractors: Providing quick energy for movement
Helping regulate your temperature
Keeping bones flexible
explanation: Protein is building material rather than fuel. Your hair, nails, skin and muscles are all largely built from it — which is why it's the one your body is reluctant to burn for energy.

question: Where is most of your body's calcium stored?
answer: In your bones and teeth
distractors: In your blood
In your muscle tissue
In your skin and hair
explanation: Your skeleton holds the overwhelming majority, doubling as a storage bank your body draws on when blood levels need topping up. Bone is a structure and a warehouse at the same time.

question: Does the water in food count toward what you drink?
answer: Yes — fruit, vegetables and soup all add to it
distractors: No, only plain water counts toward it
Only if the food is served cold
Only in small amounts not worth counting
explanation: A cucumber is over 95% water and a watermelon isn't far behind. A decent share of most people's daily fluid arrives on a plate rather than in a glass.

question: What does fiber do?
answer: It gives everything else something to move along with
distractors: It's slowly digested, which releases energy steadily
It absorbs water, which is what keeps you feeling full
It binds to minerals so they can be taken up
explanation: Fiber is the part of a plant you don't digest, and that's exactly the point — it gives the rest something to travel with. It does hold water too, but the moving-along is the main job.

question: Besides water, what does your body lose most of in sweat?
answer: Salt
distractors: Sugar
Protein
Calcium
explanation: That's why sweat tastes salty, and why a dried shirt can show faint white marks after a hot day. On an ordinary day you replace it without thinking about it, from food.

question: Which of these is a mineral your body needs?
answer: Iron
distractors: Protein
Fiber
Starch
explanation: Iron sits at the center of the molecule that carries oxygen in your blood — there's genuinely a little metal involved in every breath. Protein, fiber and starch are all things your body needs too; they're just not minerals.

question: Where does most food absorption actually happen?
answer: The small intestine
distractors: The stomach
The large intestine
The mouth
explanation: The stomach mostly does the breaking down. The small intestine does the absorbing, through a lining folded so densely that its surface area is enormous for something that fits inside you.

question: Why does your stomach rumble?
answer: Muscles squeezing gas and fluid along your digestive tract
distractors: The stomach contracting on itself because it's empty
Air you swallowed with food working its way back up
Acid sloshing about with nothing in there to work on
explanation: Those muscles squeeze all day, full or empty. It's simply louder when there's less food in there to muffle it — so a rumble isn't really a hunger signal, it's a volume change.

question: What happens to your fluid needs when you're active or it's hot?
answer: They go up, because more fluid is leaving
distractors: They stay about the same — the body compensates
They go down, because you're using water more efficiently
They change only if you're active for over an hour
explanation: More sweat means more leaving, so more needs replacing. There's no single right number for anyone — it moves with the day you're actually having, which is why drinking to thirst plus a bit works better than counting glasses.

question: What does warming up actually do?
answer: Raises muscle temperature and gets blood flowing
distractors: Uses up energy you'd otherwise have for the session
Loosens muscle by lengthening it before the work starts
Mainly prepares your mind rather than your body
explanation: Warm muscle contracts more easily and stretches further than cold muscle. The name is completely literal. It does help your head as well, but the temperature part is real and measurable.

question: When does soreness from unfamiliar exercise usually peak?
answer: A day or two afterwards
distractors: Immediately, as you finish
Within a couple of hours
About a week later
explanation: The delay is the confusing part. You can finish feeling perfectly fine and wake up thirty-six hours later wondering what happened — which is why the culprit is usually the session before last, not the last one.

question: What do most people find helps mild soreness feel better?
answer: Gentle movement
distractors: Complete stillness for a couple of days
A harder session, to push through it
Keeping the muscle completely unused
explanation: Easy movement tends to loosen sore muscles, which is why the first few minutes of a gentle walk often feel worse than the last few. Nothing here needs to be earned back — it's just circulation.

question: Is soreness a good measure of how useful a workout was?
answer: No — plenty of effective sessions leave none at all
distractors: Yes — more soreness reliably means more was achieved
Only for people new to the movement
Only for strength work, not for walking or cycling
explanation: Soreness mostly tracks novelty, not value. Try a movement you've never done and you'll feel it; that doesn't make it better than one you're used to. Beginners do get more of it, which is exactly why it's a bad measure of progress.

question: What's the point of a cool-down?
answer: Letting your heart rate come down gradually with easy movement
distractors: Stretching everything you used while it's still warm
Getting your breathing back to normal as fast as possible
Sitting down straight away, so recovery can start
explanation: Easing off gives your circulation a few minutes to settle rather than going from full effort to a chair in one step. The stretching part is optional — pleasant, but not what a cool-down is for.

question: Why does a warm-up often use the same movements as the workout?
answer: It rehearses the pattern, so your nervous system is ready
distractors: It's mainly tradition, carried over from competitive sport
It saves time compared with a separate warm-up
It uses fewer muscles, which is why it tires you less
explanation: A warm-up isn't only about temperature. A lighter version of what's coming tunes up the timing and coordination you're about to need, so the first proper rep isn't the first time your body has seen the movement today.

question: What happens inside a joint when you move it gently before exercise?
answer: Joint fluid spreads over the surfaces
distractors: The cartilage softens slightly as it warms
Extra fluid is produced and fills the joint
The bone ends separate, giving a little more room
explanation: Joints get their lubrication from movement itself — a few gentle circles spread the fluid where it's needed. Nothing at all happens while you sit still, which is most of why stiffness eases a few minutes into a walk.

question: How much does getting fitter depend on a session hurting?
answer: Hardly at all — most progress happens without any pain
distractors: A great deal — discomfort is the signal that something changed
It depends: strength needs pain, flexibility does not
Only for beginners, who have the most adapting to do
explanation: Steady, unremarkable sessions build more over a year than occasional punishing ones. Effort and pain aren't the same currency, and treating them as one is how people end up injured or, more often, put off.

question: What usually happens to soreness the second time you do the same workout?
answer: It's usually much less
distractors: It's usually a little worse
It's much the same each time
It moves to different muscles
explanation: It's called the repeated bout effect, and it's fast: your muscles adapt to that specific challenge often after a single exposure. The second time is the evidence that the first time did something.

question: Why do cold days often call for a longer warm-up?
answer: Muscles start out cooler, so there's further to go
distractors: Cold air carries less oxygen, so you tire sooner
Blood moves more slowly in the cold
Joints hold less fluid at low temperatures
explanation: You're starting further from where you need to be. The warm-up's job hasn't changed; it just has more distance to cover. Cold air oxygen is a common belief and isn't the issue — the air is the same air.

question: What's the difference between being out of breath and being sore?
answer: One is your heart and lungs, the other is your muscles
distractors: One comes during the session, the other always after it
One is a sign of effort, the other a sign of damage
They're two names for the same experience
explanation: You can be gasping with perfectly fresh legs, or breathing easily with aching thighs. They're two separate systems reporting separately, and improving one doesn't automatically improve the other.

question: What is a 'warm-up set'?
answer: An easier version of the exercise, done first
distractors: The hardest set, done while you're freshest
A set done at the end, to finish the muscle off
A stretch held before the exercise begins
explanation: It lets you practice the exact movement while it still feels easy, so the working sets aren't the first time your body has seen that pattern today. Cheap insurance, and it takes about a minute.

question: What does a bout of activity tend to do to mood?
answer: Lift it, often within minutes
distractors: Lift it, but only after several weeks
Lower it briefly, then lift it hours later
Change it only if the session was long enough
explanation: The mood lift usually arrives faster than people expect — well before any change in fitness. It's the quickest return movement offers, and it doesn't wait for you to get good at anything.

question: What can a short burst of movement do for concentration?
answer: Sharpen attention for a while afterwards
distractors: Sharpen attention, but only during the movement itself
Use up focus that you'd otherwise have for the task
Help children more than adults, whose attention is already set
explanation: The lift lands after you sit back down, which is what makes it useful. A short walk before something you've been avoiding is one of the cheapest focus tricks there is, and it works at any age.

question: What did the research on walking and ideas actually find?
answer: More ideas while walking, and shortly after sitting down
distractors: Logic problems solved faster while walking than sitting
Better recall of what had been read while walking
Better decisions when people walked before deciding
explanation: The well-known study looked at one specific thing — coming up with lots of ideas — and found walking helped, indoors on a treadmill as much as outdoors. Why is still open; "the body's on autopilot so the mind wanders" is a reasonable guess rather than a finding.

question: Roughly what share of your body's energy does your brain use?
answer: About a fifth
distractors: About a fiftieth
About half
Almost none
explanation: Your brain is about 2% of your weight and uses roughly a fifth of your energy. Easily the most expensive organ you own, and it costs much the same whether you're solving something difficult or staring out of a window.

question: Which part of the brain helps make movement smooth?
answer: The cerebellum, at the back and bottom
distractors: The frontal lobe, behind your forehead
The spinal cord, which handles the timing
The inner ear, which coordinates with the muscles
explanation: The cerebellum is about a tenth of your brain by volume and holds more than half its neurons. Making a movement smooth turns out to be a genuinely enormous calculation.

question: Where does 'muscle memory' actually live?
answer: In brain and nerve pathways
distractors: In the muscle fibers themselves
In the tendons connecting muscle to bone
In the spinal cord, separately from the brain
explanation: Muscles store nothing; they do as they're told. What practice changes is the pathway sending the instructions — which is why riding a bike survives a decade off one, and why the name is a good description in the wrong place.

question: What's happening when a movement becomes automatic?
answer: Your brain has bundled the steps into one pattern
distractors: The movement has transferred from brain to muscle
You've stopped needing to pay attention to the outcome
The steps happen faster than your brain can follow
explanation: It's called chunking: twenty separate instructions get bundled into one. It's why tying a shoelace takes no thought at all and explaining it out loud is surprisingly hard.

question: What's the link between regular activity and memory?
answer: Regular activity is linked to better memory over time
distractors: Activity helps recall on the day, but not over time
The link exists only in older adults
Only mentally demanding activity is linked to memory
explanation: The part of the brain most involved in forming memories is also one of the areas most responsive to regular movement — and it's ordinary activity that shows up in the studies, not anything clever.

question: Why does your heart speed up before a race even starts?
answer: Your brain prepares your body ahead of the effort
distractors: Small muscle movements have already started without you noticing
Nervousness raises heart rate by a separate route entirely
Your breathing changed first, and the heart followed
explanation: Your body starts the preparation before the first step, anticipating the demand rather than waiting to be surprised by it. It's the same machinery behind nerves before anything that matters.

question: How fast do nerve signals travel to your muscles?
answer: Well over 100 miles per hour
distractors: About the speed of a fast walk
Roughly the speed of sound in air
Effectively the speed of light
explanation: The fastest nerves carry signals at over 200 miles per hour, along a wire made of cells. Fast — but nowhere near light, which is why there's always a small delay between deciding and moving.

question: What do endorphins do?
answer: Chemicals your body makes that dull pain and lift mood
distractors: The chemicals that make a muscle actually contract
They carry oxygen to the muscle during hard effort
They're released to raise your heart rate before exercise
explanation: The name is a squashed-together version of "endogenous morphine" — a painkiller your own body makes. They're part of why a hard effort can leave you feeling better than it had any right to.

question: Why can music make a workout feel easier?
answer: It pulls attention away from effort and gives you a rhythm to move to
distractors: It raises your heart rate, so the work needs less of your own drive
It relaxes the muscles, so the same movement costs less
It slows your breathing, which makes the effort feel steadier
explanation: The work doesn't change — how hard it feels does. People reliably rate the same effort as easier with music playing, and a beat you can move to does a bit more than one you can't.

question: What's the largest organ in the human body?
answer: The skin
distractors: The liver
The lungs
The gut
explanation: Skin counts as an organ, and it's the biggest one you have: waterproof, self-repairing and temperature-regulating, wrapped around everything else. The liver is the largest internal one.

question: How often does the outer layer of your skin replace itself?
answer: Roughly every month
distractors: Roughly every week
Roughly every year
It doesn't — the cells last a lifetime
explanation: New cells push up from below and the old ones flake off at the top. The skin you can see now isn't the skin you'll be wearing next season, which is also why scrapes heal so readily.

question: Which is true about your fingerprints?
answer: They form before birth and never change pattern
distractors: They finish forming during early childhood
They change slowly as your hands get used
They're inherited, so close relatives share them
explanation: The ridges are set months before you're born and the pattern never changes — it just gets bigger as your hands grow. Identical twins have different ones, because the pattern isn't only genetic.

question: What's the hardest substance in your body?
answer: Tooth enamel
distractors: Bone
Fingernail
The cartilage in your ears
explanation: Enamel is harder than bone, and it is the one part of you with no living cells in it — so once it is gone it cannot grow back. It can be topped up, though: minerals from saliva and toothpaste move back into enamel that has started to soften, which is most of what brushing is for.

question: Are most people slightly taller in the morning?
answer: Yes — the discs in your spine compress over the day
distractors: Yes, but only after a day spent on your feet
No — height is fixed once you've stopped growing
Only children, whose spines are still soft
explanation: The soft discs between your vertebrae squash a little under a day of gravity and plump back up overnight. Astronauts gain a couple of inches for the same reason, and lose it again on the way home.

question: How many neck bones does a giraffe have compared to you?
answer: The same — seven
distractors: Far more, because of the length
Far fewer, but each is enormous
Roughly double what you have
explanation: Almost every mammal has exactly seven neck vertebrae — mice, humans and giraffes alike. A giraffe's are simply each about as long as your forearm.

question: What are goosebumps left over from?
answer: Ancestors with more hair, fluffing it up for warmth
distractors: A way of reducing heat loss by tightening the skin
Tiny cramps in the muscles just under the skin
A warning signal that the skin is too cold
explanation: A tiny muscle at the base of each hair pulls it upright. On a furry animal that traps a layer of warm air; on us it just makes bumps. It's a working system attached to equipment we no longer have.

question: What causes your fingers to wrinkle in a long bath?
answer: A nerve-driven change in the blood vessels under the skin
distractors: The outer layer swelling as it absorbs water
Oils being washed out, which lets the skin fold
Warm water expanding the skin faster than it can flatten
explanation: It was assumed for years to be simple soaking, and it isn't — your nervous system does it deliberately. A finger whose nerve supply is damaged won't wrinkle at all, which is how anyone found out.

question: Which sense is most closely wired to memory?
answer: Smell
distractors: Hearing
Touch
Taste
explanation: Smell signals take an unusually short route to the memory regions of the brain, skipping a relay the other senses go through. It's why one unexpected scent can drop you into a specific afternoon from twenty years ago.

question: What happens to your skeleton over the years?
answer: It's gradually replaced, a little at a time, for life
distractors: It stops changing once you've finished growing
It hardens steadily and is never removed
Only the outer surface is renewed
explanation: Old bone is removed and new bone laid down continuously, so the skeleton you have isn't made of the same material it was a decade ago. It's a structure being rebuilt while it's still in use.

question: Which part of your body has no blood supply of its own?
answer: The cornea, at the front of your eye
distractors: The lens, sitting just behind it
The outer layer of your skin
The enamel on the outside of your teeth
explanation: The cornea has to stay perfectly clear, and blood vessels would get in the way. It takes oxygen straight from the air through the tear film, and its nutrients from the fluid just behind it.

question: What causes the popping sound when a knuckle cracks?
answer: A gas bubble forming in the joint fluid
distractors: The bone surfaces sliding past one another
A ligament snapping briefly over a bone
Air being drawn in from outside the joint
explanation: Scans of joints as they crack show a bubble appearing in the joint fluid at the exact moment of the pop. It takes a while to reset, which is why you can't do the same knuckle twice in a row.

question: Which is the longest nerve in your body?
answer: The sciatic, from the lower back down
distractors: The optic, from the eye to the brain
The one running the length of the arm
The one running down the spine itself
explanation: It runs from your lower back down toward your foot, and at its widest it's about as thick as your thumb. The spinal cord is thicker, but that's a bundle rather than a single nerve.

question: What does 'making it obvious' mean for a habit?
answer: Setting up cues, like leaving your shoes by the door
distractors: Telling people about it, so you feel accountable
Putting it somewhere in the day where there's room
Choosing something you'll enjoy enough to remember
explanation: Habits respond to what's physically in front of you. Shoes by the door and a bottle on the desk do more work than willpower does — the other three all help, but none of them is what "obvious" is pointing at.

question: Which builds consistency better?
answer: A small action you'll actually repeat
distractors: A demanding action you'll manage now and then
Whichever one you feel most motivated about
The one that fits best once everything else is settled
explanation: Five minutes done forty times beats an hour done twice. Repetition is the ingredient; size is just the flavouring. Waiting for motivation or for a clear week both put the starting date somewhere in the future.

question: What usually helps a habit survive a disruption like travel?
answer: Having a smaller version you can still do
distractors: Making up the missed days once you're home
Pausing it deliberately, with a date to resume
Swapping it for something else while you're away
explanation: A two-minute version keeps the thread intact, and it's far easier to scale a habit back up than to restart one from nothing. Making up missed days sounds conscientious and mostly just makes returning feel expensive.

question: Which is true about motivation?
answer: It usually follows action rather than leading it
distractors: It has to be there before you'll manage to start
It builds steadily the longer you keep a habit
It's fairly stable, and varies mostly between people
explanation: Most people expect to feel like it first. In practice, starting is usually what generates the feeling — the first two minutes do the convincing, which is why "just put your shoes on" is better advice than it sounds.

question: What is a streak most useful for?
answer: Taking the daily decision out of it
distractors: Giving you something to measure your progress against
Making the habit harder to abandon once it's long
Showing how fit you've become over time
explanation: The real cost of a habit is deciding about it every single day. A streak quietly settles that question. It isn't a fitness measurement, and a long one shouldn't be the reason you keep going — that turns a helpful thing into a debt.

question: Why does a fixed time or place help a habit stick?
answer: The situation itself starts acting as the reminder
distractors: Repetition at a set time trains the body to expect it
It's easier to defend a slot other people know about
Fixed routines take less energy than flexible ones
explanation: After enough repetitions, walking into the kitchen at seven is the prompt. You stop needing to remember, because the room remembers for you — which is a different mechanism from your body learning a schedule.

question: How does a habit usually feel after several weeks of repeating it?
answer: Starting it takes less mental effort than it did
distractors: The action itself becomes physically easier
It feels much the same, but you mind it less
It becomes automatic enough to do without noticing
explanation: The action doesn't get easier — the starting does. That drop in friction is what people mean when they say something has become a habit, and it's why a hard session can still feel hard years in.

question: How long does it take to form a habit?
answer: It varies a lot by person and by habit
distractors: About three weeks, for most people
About two months, for most people
It depends mainly on how often you repeat it
explanation: The famous 21-day figure was never a research finding — it came from a surgeon's observation about patients adjusting after an operation. When it was actually studied, the spread between people ran from under three weeks to the better part of a year.

question: What does tracking a habit tend to do?
answer: It turns the effort into something you can look at
distractors: It shows you which days of the week are your strongest
It makes the habit feel more like an obligation
It mainly helps people who are consistent already
explanation: A visible record turns an invisible effort into something you can look at, and people are reliably more willing to continue a line they can see. Worth noticing when it tips into obligation, though — that's the point to shorten the line, not the habit.

question: What's a realiztic way to restart after a long break?
answer: Begin below where you left off
distractors: Pick up roughly where you stopped
Start with your hardest session, to prove you still can
Wait for a natural restarting point, like a new month
explanation: Starting under your old level almost always gets you back faster, because the easy first week is the one that actually happens. Picking up where you stopped is the common instinct and the usual reason the restart lasts four days.

question: Why do 'all or nothing' plans often fall apart?
answer: They turn one imperfect day into total failure
distractors: They ask for more time than most people have
They get boring long before they become a habit
